Diego to schedule 1hr deep-dive with platform team for egress testing week of 2027-11-29

summary: Initial intake to scope a Private deployment. Customer has strict egress controls and an outbound proxy. They want a plan for private endpoints, peering topology, and how Redwood integrates with their KMS and audit requirements.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Martinez (Redwood SE); Aisha Patel (Cedarcrest Head of Cloud); Tom Nguyen (Infosec); Leah Brooks (Platform); Raj Mehta (DevOps)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Diego our solutions engineer. Appreciate you carving time.
[00:08] Aisha: hey thanks, quick housekeeping, Tom's on mute but he'll be chiming in on security. we're trying to narrow down network constraints for a private deployment.
[00:15] Diego: great, we usually start with your current VPC layout, egress model (proxy or direct), and whether you need inter-region peering — that helps us recommend private endpoints vs. peering.
[00:30] Leah: quick context, we run most services in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, primary data residency need is that logs and request metadata for certain customers must stay in eu-west-1. we also force all outbound through a corporate proxy in a central NAT VPC.
[00:45] Tom: and we have strict egress allow lists. nothing goes out direct to internet without proxy inspection, we also require TLS terminated at our proxy sometimes.
[00:52] Maya: ok that's helpful. Two broad patterns we see: 1) Redwood Private with VPC peering/transit gateway to your VPCs and private endpoints inside your account; or 2) PrivateLink-style private endpoints where Redwood exposes an interface endpoint and customer connects in. Each has tradeoffs on routing, egress, and IP management.
[01:10] Raj: can you explain differences for traffic flow? how does egress look for token validation and model fetches?
[01:18] Diego: sure. For peering/transit, all traffic is routed over internal networks — so if you have egress through your proxy, outbound still hits the proxy when configured. For PrivateLink (interface endpoints), traffic terminates at the ENI in your VPC and we still call back to control plane over private connectivity, but management/control-plane may require limited internet egress or a peered control plane depending on mode.
[01:40] Aisha: we can't have anything reaching a public internet IP from our VPC except through the proxy. is that feasible?
[01:46] Diego: yes, that's a common pattern. Redwood Private can be deployed inside your account or in a dedicated VPC peered to yours. In both cases egress rules can be preserved — you would route outbound to the proxy. If we host components in a Redwood-managed VPC, we'd ask for specific allowlist ranges for control-plane callbacks.
[02:08] Tom: what about KMS — we must keep encryption keys in our HSM and cannot share with external tenants.
[02:14] Maya: we support customer-managed KMS in Private deployments. For on-prem or VPC installs we can integrate with your KMS/HSM; there are different patterns depending on whether it's a fully customer-managed control plane or a hybrid where Redwood manages certain infra.
[02:30] Leah: we're also concerned about egress to model registries. If you do rolling updates, does Redwood fetch model blobs from internet S3 buckets?
[02:38] Diego: good callout. For Private we can sync model artifacts into your S3 (pull mode) or have a private repo in your account. We can also push model fleet images into your ECR. That avoids any direct internet egress for model pulls.
[02:55] [03:00] Aisha: timings — we want to pilot in us-east-1 first, then eu-west-1. For eu-west-1 we need architecture that guarantees request metadata does not leave eu-west-1. how do you handle regional routing?
[03:12] Maya: we can pin model servers and control routing by region. In practice you would provision Redwood nodes in eu-west-1 and set a routing policy so those requests stay local. For analytics/telemetry we also offer region-specific retention and can disable cross-region log export.
[03:30] Raj: firewall rules — our security team wants to avoid adding lots of CIDR entries. is there a way to use private endpoints with a small set of IPs?
[03:38] Diego: PrivateLink gives you a set of ENIs which have stable IPs in your subnets. If we need minimal allowlist footprint, we can recommend interface endpoints or use a transit gateway + NVA with a single egress path. If you choose Redwood-managed VPC, we typically provide an allowlist of CIDRs.
[04:00] Tom: any dependencies on service mesh or sidecars? we have an mTLS mesh in prod.
[04:06] Maya: Redwood runtime doesn't require a service mesh on your side but it can integrate. If you have egress mTLS enforced by sidecars, we can route traffic through your mesh, though there may be additional configuration for certs and SNI.
[04:25] Leah: we have an outbound proxy that terminates TLS and inspects traffic; that breaks end-to-end TLS to Redwood unless we allow tunneling. do you support proxy authentication or CONNECT tunneling?
[04:34] Diego: we support outbound CONNECT tunnels and can also accept calls over TLS from within the VPC. If the proxy intercepts TLS, we prefer that it allows CONNECT so the client can negotiate. For control-plane callbacks we can also use a private peering so you avoid proxy interception.
[04:55] [05:00] Maya: let's talk about maintenance windows and failover. if we host in eu-west-1 and us-east-1, how does failover behave and how do you ensure data residency?
[05:10] Diego: you map routes per workload. For strict residency, you pin both serving and logging to region. For failover we can do regional fallback but you can opt-out for sensitive datasets. For non-sensitive traffic we can failover to another region.
[05:30] Aisha: audit logs — we need full request traces for compliance and immutable logs stored for 7 years. can Redwood stream logs to our S3/GCS?
[05:40] Maya: yes, Redwood can export audit logs to your object storage inside the same region. We can also send to your SIEM over private connection. Logs can be PII-scrubbed or redacted based on rules.
[05:58] Raj: latency — we benchmarked some hosted APIs earlier; for production we need sub-120ms p95 for short prompts. does private deployment introduce overhead?
[06:10] Diego: usually private has negligible overhead; the main latency contributors are network hop and any proxy inspection. If you avoid TLS interception and keep traffic local in-region, you should match hosted performance.
[06:30] [06:45] Tom: legal question — we need contract language about data deletion and ephemeral KV cache clearing on certin triggers. can you support automated cache wipe?
[06:53] Maya: yes, we have API hooks to flush KV caches and data retention policies that can be enforced on the Private control plane. We'll surface contract language in our security packet.
[07:10] Leah: about private endpoints — do we need to open inbound rules in our firewall to accept connections from your fleet? or do you terminate connections from our side?
[07:18] Diego: with peering the traffic is initiated from your side to the model servers in the peered VPC (or vice versa depending on design). For PrivateLink, the interface endpoint accepts connections inside your VPC — you control the subnet and security groups. We typically recommend customer-initiated connections so you can enforce SGs and NSGs.
[07:40] Aisha: we have an existing transit gateway and prefer to avoid adding more peering links. can Redwood attach to our TGW?
[07:48] Diego: yes, we can connect via TGW attachments. That works well for multi-account setups; we can map route tables so only specific subnets reach Redwood nodes.
[08:00] Maya: good to call out: for TGW you'll want to plan route propagation and ensure we don't accidentally learn routes to sensitive subnets. We recommend a dedicated segment for inference nodes.
[08:20] [08:30] Tom: on compliance, do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001? and do you do pen tests?
[08:36] Maya: we have SOC 2 Type II and perform annual external pen tests. We'll include certs and the latest report in the security pack.
[08:50] Raj: small detail — we use a particular proxy that requires client certs for outbound. can Redwood present a client cert?
[08:58] Diego: yes, we can configure client-side certs in the private deployment or provide a mutual TLS termination option if you're doing proxy auth. We'll need the CA chain and cert rotation policies.
[09:20] Leah: EKS vs. plain VMs for your runtime? we run in EKS and want to know how we should host Redwood nodes.
[09:27] Diego: we support multiple deployment patterns. For Private we often recommend managed nodes (VMs) for GPU infra, but if you're on EKS with GPU node groups you can host containers. We'll share an ops runbook for both.
[09:42] Maya: let's carve out a checklist of what we need from you to scope a pilot.
[09:47] Aisha: sure.
[09:50] Maya: 1) list of target regions and subnets for pilot; 2) egress proxy config and CA chains; 3) KMS/HSM contact and whether keys are customer-managed; 4) sample workloads and SLOs; 5) allowlist ranges if you prefer Redwood-managed VPC.
[10:10] Leah: we can provide regions and subnets by Friday. proxy config might take longer as it touches the security team.
[10:18] Tom: we'll need the security pack before we commit to a pilot.
[10:21] Maya: understood, we'll send the pack today and follow up with the runbook and diagram.
[10:26] [10:30] Diego: one more technical note on model artifacts: if you want to avoid cross-region transfers, we can replicate artifacts into your S3 in each region. That avoids external egress.
[10:40] Raj: licensing and pricing — high level, how do you price Private vs Dedicated?
[10:46] Maya: Private has a platform fee plus instance/GPU costs. Dedicated reserved capacity is a commitment model. We'll send a tailored pricing sheet after we understand required size for pilot.
[10:58] [11:00] Aisha: any blockers we should know about?
[11:03] Diego: not from a tech side; main lift is networking/allowlist work and KMS integration approvals.
[11:10] Leah: can you show us a sample peering route table?
[11:13] Diego: yes we'll include sample route tables and security group templates in the follow-up.
[11:22] Maya: ok, quick recap and next steps?
[11:25] Aisha: recap: send security docs, sample network diagrams, cost estimate, and schedule a deep-dive.
[11:31] Maya: exactly — Maya will send the security packet and initial diagrams by 11/24; Diego will set up the week-of 11/29 deep-dive for egress testing. Cedarcrest to provide subnet list and proxy details by 11/26.
[11:45] Tom: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:48] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up via email with next steps and calendar invites.
[11:55] [12:00] End of call. Some transcription notes: occasional filler words and overlap. Some proper nouns (internal product names) may be mis-transcribed.
